The Power of Pollen

By: Anina Peens | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Too small to see with the naked eye, pollen can assist in solving crime while it has in itself the power to kill

Unique Selling Point:
Palynology is a word most South Africans have never heard of. It is the fascinating world of how the plant reproductive system aids in solving crimes, while the understanding and awareness of pollen cycles, can also save lives.

Summary:
Forensic palynology is an entirely new method for solving crime in South Africa. By tracing pollen spores, forensic teams can identify the location of crime scenes, trace evidence to its source, determine the travel history of illicit drugs, poached animal parts, forged documentation and locate unidentified human remains. Palynologists warn that pollen counts are drastically increasing as a result of global warming and that pollen related allergies and asthma attacks will significantly increase in the next few years.

Further information:
Story Elements

1. Introduction to Pollen
- It is one of the smallest materials visible to the human eye
- The use of a graphic explains the tiny material with the power to solve crimes and kill people.

2. Nature trumps crime

- We are at the UCT Lung institute where Prof Jonny Peters introduces forensic palynology.
- He explains how pollen are taken from objects such as clothing, to the microscope and how it is analyzed.
- We see the pollen under the microscope and how different variants are detected.
- Case study: Explanation of the Knysna case. What evidence were collected and how was it traced? Possible reenactment of evidence.
- Introduce Patricia Wiltshire via Zoom from the UK who have worked with the police on over 300 cases of forensic palynology.

3. What we have and what we need

- There are no forensic palynologists in South Africa although there are palynologists who specialize in fossil palynology and the database, they have been building up has been helpful for forensic palynologists as well as aerobiologists.
- Introducing Lynn Quick who talks about fossil pollen and how that can assist forensic palynologists.

4. The importance of data basis

- We look at a pollen trap and how it works. What is the importance of a pollen trap and how up to now, South Africa only had one. But now there are seven. Pollen trap expert Bosco Weliyala takes us onto a rooftop and shows us how the traps work.


5. But Pollen itself has the power to kill

- Introducing Dr Dilys Berman, Aerobiologist
- She talks about the importance of awareness of the variants of pollen in South Africa.
- She mentions pollen storms in Australia and brings it back to South Africa via the Kimberley grass example.
- She stretches the importance of the data base in order to establish basis that will guide patients and diagnosis.

Script:


The Power of Pollen

VO
The case is known as one of the most elusive in British crime history. Around the turn of the century, two 10-year old girls from the town of Soham outside London… disappeared. Their bodies were found in a ditch, thirty kilometres from home. Police made no headway in identifying a murder suspect, until a forensic palynologist examined the scene…and the pollen spores of trees flowering in the vicinity.

SUPER@ PROF JONNY PETER, HEAD OF UCT LUNG INSTITUTE
“Palynology, the origin of the word is Greek and refers to the study of dust….”

VO
Head of the University of Cape Town’s Lung Institute, Prof Jonny Peter, is collecting pollen data to build a data base that can assist police, as in the famous British case.

SUPER@ PROF JONNY PETER, HEAD OF UCT LUNG INSTITUTE
“ If it is around a crime scene or on a suspects jersey or be that clothing on the dead body it can be used to ensure whether the body fits into that geographical area or if the body have been moved. We would know that these types of trees were flowering at a given time of year.”

LINK
Although forensic palynology has been used as method to assist police in solving crime in other parts of the world, it has not ever really been practiced in South Africa.
We take our lead from work that has been done by world-renowned forensic palynologists of which there are only a handful globally.

VO
To date, Prof. Patricia Wiltshire has become one of the world’s most famous forensic palynologists.

SUPER@ PROF PATRICIA WILTSHIRE, BRITISH FORENSIC PALYNOLOGIST
“Basically the police will say, we know this person came to this place with the truth, or they might say we are looking for a body, and we don’t know where it is, but we have the suspect’s car, I will analyse those and from the palynological profile I would get, place would form in my mind”

VO
Wiltshire’s knowledge of palynology combined with her extensive training in ecology and botany has helped the British police solve more than 300 cases.

LINK
(FLORIS, SIT ASB N REPEAT VAN DIE TWEE DOGTERTJIES SE VISUALS HIER SODAT ONS DIE LINK KAN MAAK DAT DIT DIE SAAK IS WAARVAN ONS PRAAT IN DIE BEGIN VAN DIE STORIE)
Professor Wiltshire is the palynologist who solved the Soham murder case. She led the police to the killer by tracing the pollen spores found on the evidence.

SUPER@ PROF PATRICIA WILTSHIRE, BRITISH FORENSIC PALYNOLOGIST
ZOOM INTERVIEW 12’04
“I Showed that he took the clothes off the girls while they were in the ditch, I showed the police how he got into the ditch and I showed he went into the ditch twice. And I did that straight from the botany and also from the palynology on his footwear and his car.”

VO
Back at home, experts know of only one criminal case that’s been solved using forensic palynology

SUPER@ PROF JONNY PETER, HEAD OF UCT LUNG INSTITUTE
“In Knysna, a body was shown to have been moved based on the pollen that was found on the body”

LINK
The reasons why forensic palynology is not known or practised in South Africa is not only because of a lack of skills but also a major lack of pollen data that indicate the types of pollen that occur specific areas during specific times of the year.

VO
In the UK, Wiltshire says, resources in Britain are well established.

SUPER@ PROF PATRICIA WILTSHIRE, BRITISH FORENSIC PALYNOLOGIST
“We are lucky in Brittan because the vegetation is mapped, we got wonderful data basis in Britain, but we can’t say that of the rest of the world.”

VO
But her knowledge of pollen and vegetation was built over many years of hands-on experience.

SUPER@ PROF PATRICIA WILTSHIRE, BRITISH FORENSIC PALYNOLOGIST
“I have been all over Britain doing fieldworks, walking and digging in swamps, so I have a very good idea of what is there. Very difficult in Africa, such a big place. So I think in Africa you would have to regionalise.”

VO
One way to collect pollen data is by setting pollen traps. Although the traps are developed for medical research, they collect data that can be applied in any forensic investigation

MASA Link:
“The trap is designed to simulate human breathing patterns to determine the amount of air that enters a person’s lungs on a daily basis. The trap pulls in 10 litres of air per minute, which is relatively the same as a human being.

VO
Dr Dilys Berman is an aerobiologist – she works with pollen traps designed in the UK, that collects samples from the air in 24-hour cycles. She resets the trap every seven days.


SUPER@ DR DYLIS BERMAN, AEROBIOLOGIST
“The air flows over this specially prepared strip and traps pollen and fungal spores.”
INSERT BYTE
“we now have seven cities in the country that we are monitoring the different biomes.”

VO
Extracting the pollen from the trap installed at the Cape Town astrological observatory, the team analyses and logs the findings in their lab at Groote Schuur hospital.

MASA:
“So now we have pollen from the strip and we are in the lab, what happens next?”

SUPER@ DR NANIKA ESTERHUIZE, PALYNOLOGIST.
“Now that we have taken from the trap, we bring it back to the lab and we make slides from those strips. This is a cutting block we use to represent certain segments of specific days. So after you.. .then you can identify and count the different pollen grains from different plant species, because the pollen from different plant species look completely different under a microscope so you can identify the different plants where pollen comes from.

VO
At the moment there are only seven pollen traps in South Africa’s largest cities, but UCT plans to expand those, so they could monitor all the different plant communities and vegetation types across the country.

SUPER@ PROF JONNY PETER, HEAD OF UCT LUNG INSTITUTE
“You cannot monitor pollen in Cape town and say what is going on in Joburg. As a result what we are putting together and we are trying to grow this initiative is something called, the South African pollen monitoring network.”

VO
It’s not only pollen from the present that tells a story: From water bodies, grasslands and deserts, fossil palynologists like Dr Lynne Quick – one of very few in Africa – are able to dig up and identify pollen spores that date back millions of years.

SUPER@DR LYNNE QUICK, FOSSIL POLLEN EXPERT
“The good thing about pollen and the species that we are looking at and the genes and families we are looking at, is that they haven’t changed, so I can find the same type of plant over thousands or ten thousands of years that we are seeing today back in time and that is how I can tie in what type of climates and environments we are looking at.”

VO
Quick says it’s the very structure of pollen molecules that makes them ideal for forensic inquiries.


UPSOUND
MASA: So, Pollen does not age and it does not evolve?”

SUPER@DR LYNNE QUICK, FOSSIL POLLEN EXPERT
“The great thing about pollen is the fact that it preserves so well because of that outer layer. It is one of the most inert chemical compound that we know of and that is why it is so useful in crime scenes or to go back in the past to look at the last ice age”

VO
Although pollen research is slowly expanding in South Africa, the lack of experts in the field remains the greatest challenge.

SUPER@ PROF JONNY PETER, HEAD OF UCT LUNG INSTITUTE
“We are trying to grow that network by training young scientists that are interested in pollen and also connecting with other fields like fossilised pollen and those scientists can help us to read modern pollen.

LINK
The university of Cape Town is the only university in Africa that is focussed on developing this research. For this reasons, medics and scientists from other African countries come here for training.

VO
Kenyan Dr Evelyn Nganga is specialising in children’s allergies. Her training with the team at UCT will make her one of the fellow pioneers, working to expand the expertise of palynologists across Africa.


CHANGE STRAP
SUPER@ PROF EVELYN NGANGA, NAIROBI- BASED PEDIATRIC ALLERGORIST
“It is my hope that with this training and what I have acquired while I have been here is that I will be able to identify and do a data base of conditions we are seeing in East Africa. Because as it stands, only South Africa is able to do that kind of pollen monitoring and I think there are a few traps in Nigeria, which seems to be the representation of Africa, which I think is a underrepresentation so we hoping that could change.
